hints: Break the word apart - homeo means similar or same and stasis means staying. Think about what part of the body must be kept steady despite outside changes.
walkthrough:
What Needs Staying Steady**
Think of your cells sitting in tissue fluid. Enzymes and membranes only work well if conditions like temperature, pH, water potential and glucose stay almost the same, even when the outside world changes.

Putting The Definition Together**
So homeostasis is not keeping one thing fixed forever, it is actively maintaining the internal environment constant around a set point, correcting any drift back within narrow limits by negative feedback.
Final answer: The maintenance of a constant / stable internal environment within narrow limits / around a set point.

hints: Look at A first. It points to the large white funnel-shaped space in the centre where all the collecting ducts empty urine before it leaves the kidney.
Now follow the flow out of that funnel. B points to the tube that carries urine away from the kidney down toward the bladder.
walkthrough:
Reading The Diagram**
The centre of the section shows a branched cavity. That is where urine from many nephrons is collected together. Around it is the solid kidney tissue with cortex outside and medulla inside.

Naming A and B**
A points into that central collecting funnel, which is the pelvis. It funnels urine into B, the single muscular tube leaving the kidney, which is the ureter leading to the bladder.
Final answer: A - pelvis (renal pelvis); B - ureter.

hints: Start with what each process needs. Ultrafiltration needs a high-pressure capillary ball and capsule, which are only found in the outer region, while the loop of Henle needs the long straight part dipping down.
Think about the blood vessels in Fig. 1.1. One arrow brings blood in and one takes blood away. Which vessel has already passed through the kidney and had urea filtered out?
Match letters to regions: U goes to the outer cortex tissue, L goes to the inner striped medulla region, and C goes to the vessel carrying cleaned blood away.
walkthrough:
Where Ultrafiltration Happens - U**
Ultrafiltration occurs at the start of the nephron where the glomerulus sits inside the Bowman's capsule. Millions of these are packed in the cortex, the outer darker tissue. So label U with a line to the outer cortex region.

Where The Loop of Henle Is - L**
The loop of Henle is the long hairpin that drops down from the cortex into the medulla to set up the salt gradient for water reabsorption. So label L with a line to the medulla, the inner region toward the pelvis.

Where Urea Is Low - C**
Urea is filtered out of blood into the nephron and lost in urine, so blood leaving the kidney has a low urea concentration. In Fig. 1.1 the lower vessel with the arrow pointing away is the renal vein, so label C there.
Final answer: U - to the cortex (glomerulus / Bowman's capsule region); L - to the medulla; C - to the renal vein (vessel with arrow leaving kidney).

hints: Start at the sensor. Which part of the brain monitors the water potential of the blood, and what special receptor cells shrink or swell as blood gets more or less concentrated?
Think about the hormone involved. Where is ADH actually made and where is it stored and released from? Do not mix up the two parts.
Link low blood water to hormone release. What happens to ADH secretion when water potential falls, and how does the signal travel from hypothalamus to posterior pituitary?
Move to the kidney target. Which tubule parts become more permeable to water when ADH arrives, and what membrane channels are involved?
Finish with the outcome. How does more ADH change water reabsorption and the volume and concentration of urine, and what happens when ADH is low?
walkthrough:
Detecting The Change In The Hypothalamus**
The hypothalamus monitors blood water potential using osmoreceptor cells. If you are dehydrated, blood has less water so water leaves the osmoreceptors by osmosis and they shrink. That shrinkage is the signal.

Making And Releasing ADH**
ADH is made - synthesised - by nerve cells in the hypothalamus. It then travels down their axons - the neurosecretory cells - to the posterior pituitary, which stores it. When water potential is low, nerve impulses trigger release of ADH from the posterior pituitary into the blood. When water potential is high, little ADH is released.

Acting On The Kidney**
ADH travels in blood to the kidney and makes the walls of the distal convoluted tubule and especially the collecting duct more permeable to water by inserting aquaporin water channels into the cell membranes.

The Osmoregulation Outcome**
With more aquaporins, more water is reabsorbed from the tubule fluid back into the blood by osmosis. That conserves water, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced and blood water potential rises back toward normal.

Final answer: Hypothalamus contains osmoreceptors that detect water potential of blood; ADH is produced in hypothalamus and transported by neurosecretory cells to posterior pituitary; when blood water potential is low, ADH is secreted from posterior pituitary; ADH increases permeability of distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct by insertion of aquaporins, increasing water reabsorption to produce small volume of concentrated urine.
